sections.title: 1. POSITION OF AFRICA USING LINES OF LATITUDE AND LONGITUDE

blocks.x: Definitions
**Lines of latitude:** Imaginary lines drawn on a map or globe running from **east to west**, showing how far a place is north or south of the Equator.
**Lines of longitude:** Imaginary lines drawn on a map or globe running from **north to south**, showing how far a place is east or west of the Prime Meridian.
**Equator:** The line of latitude at **0°** which divides the earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
**Prime Meridian (Greenwich Meridian):** The line of longitude at **0°** which divides the earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
Explanation
To find any place on the world map, we use two numbers: one from a line of latitude and one from a line of longitude. Where the two lines cross is the position of the place.
Africa lies **between about 37°N and 35°S**, and **between about 17°W and 51°E**.

blocks.x: Definitions
**Physical features:** The land forms that exist on the earth's surface and give the land its shape.
**Relief features:** Physical features to do with the shape and height of the land, such as mountains, highlands, plateaux, lowlands, rift valleys and coastal plains.
**Drainage features:** Physical features made of water, such as rivers, lakes, seas and oceans.
Important Points

items: Physical features are **natural resources**. People depend on them to earn a living.
Some physical features form **international boundaries** — for example, Lake Victoria is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.
Physical features are formed in different ways: by **folding**, by **faulting**, by **volcanicity**, by **erosion** and by **deposition**.

blocks.x: Definitions
**Mountain:** A very high, steep area of land that rises far above the land around it.
**Highland:** A large area of land that is high above sea level but not as steep as a mountain.
The main mountains and highlands named in the syllabus

The three ways mountains are formed
**1. Folded (fold) mountains** — layers of soft rock are squeezed from both sides until they bend upwards into folds. *Examples:* Atlas Mountains, Cape Ranges of South Africa.
**2. Fault-block mountains** — the land cracks (faults) and a block of land between the cracks is pushed upwards. *Examples:* Rwenzori Mountains, Usambara Mountains.
**3. Volcanic mountains** — molten rock (magma) comes out of the earth through a weak point, cools and piles up. *Examples:* Mt Kilimanjaro, Mt Cameroon, Tibesti, Ahaggar, Mt Elgon.
Important Points

items: **Mt Kilimanjaro** is the highest mountain in Africa.
**Mt Cameroon** is the highest mountain in West Africa and is still active.
**Ras Dashen** in the Ethiopian Highlands is the highest peak in Ethiopia.
The **Atlas Mountains** protect the Mediterranean coast from the dry, dusty winds of the Sahara.

**Rift valley:** A long, deep, steep-sided valley formed when land between two parallel faults sinks.
**Depression:** A low area of land which is lower than the land around it, and sometimes lower than sea level.

blocks.x: The syllabus names six climatic regions for Africa: **Equatorial, Tropical, Desert (hot and dry), Mediterranean, Temperate** and **Montane**.
(a) Equatorial climate

items: **Where:** Along the Equator — the Congo Basin, the coast of West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana, Liberia), parts of Uganda near Lake Victoria.

**Characteristics:** Hot and wet all year; rainfall over 1,500 mm a year and falls almost daily, usually in the afternoon; temperatures about 25 °C–27 °C all year; high humidity; two rainfall peaks; heavy convectional rainfall; thick cloud cover.
**Vegetation:** Tropical rain forest.

blocks.x: (b) Tropical (savannah) climate

items: **Where:** Most of Africa north and south of the equatorial belt — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Nigeria's middle belt, Zambia, Zimbabwe.
**Characteristics:** A clear **wet season and dry season**; rainfall 750 mm–1,500 mm a year; hot for most of the year; the further from the Equator, the shorter the wet season.
**Vegetation:** Savannah grassland with scattered trees.

blocks.x: (c) Desert (hot and dry) climate

items: **Where:** The Sahara (Egypt, Libya, Algeria, Niger, Chad, Sudan, Mali, Mauritania), the Kalahari (Botswana, Namibia) and the Namib (Namibia).

**Characteristics:** Very little rainfall, below 250 mm a year; very hot during the day (over 40 °C) and very cold at night; clear skies; low humidity; strong dusty winds; a very big daily range of temperature.
**Vegetation:** Desert scrub, cacti and thorny bushes.

blocks.x: (d) Mediterranean climate

items: **Where:** The north coast of Africa — Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and northern Egypt — and the south-western tip of South Africa around Cape Town.
**Characteristics:** **Hot dry summers and warm wet winters** — the rain comes in winter; moderate rainfall of 500 mm–900 mm; plenty of sunshine.
**Vegetation:** Mediterranean vegetation — short evergreen trees and shrubs with thick bark, such as olives, cork oak, citrus and vines.

blocks.x: (e) Temperate (warm temperate) climate

items: **Where:** Parts of South Africa away from the Cape, such as the Natal coast and the high veld.
**Characteristics:** Warm summers and cool winters; moderate rainfall spread over the year; four seasons are noticed — summer, autumn, winter and spring.
**Vegetation:** Temperate grasslands called **velds**.

blocks.x: (f) Montane (mountain) climate

items: **Where:** On high mountains and highlands — Ethiopian Highlands, Mt Kilimanjaro, Mt Kenya, Rwenzori, the Atlas and Drakensberg mountains.

sections.title: 3. FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE THE CLIMATE OF AFRICA

blocks.x: (a) Latitude (distance from the Equator)

Places near the Equator receive the sun's rays almost overhead all year, so they are hot. As you move away from the Equator the rays become slanting and spread over a larger area, so it becomes cooler.
(b) Altitude (height above sea level)

The higher the place, the cooler it is. Temperature falls by about **1 °C for every 150 metres** of height. That is why the Ethiopian Highlands are cool although Ethiopia lies in the tropics, and why there is ice on Kilimanjaro even though it stands close to the Equator.
(c) Nearness to water bodies

Large lakes, seas and oceans cool the air near them during the day and warm it at night. Places near water bodies get **more rainfall** and have a **small range of temperature**. Areas far inland, like the middle of the Sahara, get little rain — this is called **continentality**.
(d) Winds
Winds carry moisture from one place to another.

blocks.x: (f) Relief and aspect

Mountains force moist air to rise. The air cools and drops its rain on the **windward side** of the mountain. The other side, called the **leeward side** or **rain shadow**, remains dry. This is how relief rainfall is formed.
(g) Vegetation
Thick forests give off water vapour into the air (transpiration). This raises humidity and brings more rainfall. Where forests are cut down, rainfall reduces.
(h) Human activities
People change climate by cutting down trees, burning bushes, draining swamps, overgrazing, mining and building factories.
(i) Land mass (size of the continent)
Africa is a very large continent. Its interior lies far from the sea, so the middle of the Sahara receives almost no moist air and is extremely dry.

sections.title: 3. MOVEMENTS OF ETHNIC GROUPS INTO AND WITHIN AFRICA

blocks.x: The main movements

items: **The Bantu migration** — from the Congo–Cameroon region the Bantu spread east and south from about A.D. 1000, reaching East Africa and later Southern Africa. Some entered Uganda through the west and settled in the fertile areas near Lake Victoria.
**The Nilotic migration** — the Luo-speaking peoples moved south along the Nile from Bahr-el-Ghazal into northern Uganda and western Kenya.
**The Nilo-Hamitic (Plain Nilote) movement** — moved south-west from the Ethiopian border into Karamoja, Teso and the Rift Valley of Kenya.
**The Cushitic movement** — came from Ethiopia southwards into northern Kenya and parts of Uganda.
**The Arab movement** — came from Arabia into North Africa and along the East African coast, mainly for trade and to spread Islam.

sections.title: 6. EUROPEAN SETTLERS AND THE GREAT TREK

blocks.x: European settlers

Some Europeans came to stay. They took the best land, especially in **South Africa**, **Zimbabwe** (then Rhodesia) and the **White Highlands of Kenya**. The Dutch (later called **Boers** or Afrikaners) first settled at the Cape in **1652** under Jan van Riebeeck. The British took over the Cape in the early 1800s.
The Great Trek
**The Great Trek** was the movement of the Boers from the Cape Colony into the interior of South Africa from about **1835**.
**Causes of the Great Trek:**

items: The Boers disliked **British rule** at the Cape.
The British **abolished slavery in 1833**, and the Boers depended on slave labour.
The Boers were not happy with the **compensation** paid for their freed slaves.
**English** was made the official language instead of Dutch.
The Boers wanted **more land** for farming and grazing.
British **laws and courts** treated Africans and Boers as equals, which the Boers rejected.
The Boers wanted **freedom to rule themselves**.

blocks.x: **Effects of the Great Trek:**

items: The Boers founded new republics — **Transvaal**, **Orange Free State** and **Natal**.
**Wars with African peoples** followed, such as the Zulu (the Battle of Blood River, 1838); Africans lost land and lives.
African communities were **displaced** and scattered.
**Gold and diamonds** were later discovered in the Boer areas, attracting more Europeans.
Conflict between the Boers and the British led to the **Anglo-Boer Wars**.
The racist attitudes of the trekkers helped to lay the foundation of **apartheid**.

The First World War (1914–1918) caused terrible destruction, so the League of Nations was formed in 1919 to keep peace — but it was weak and failed to stop aggression. The Second World War (1939–1945) killed even more people and destroyed whole cities. The nations therefore met at San Francisco and formed a stronger organisation, the United Nations, in 1945, with a Security Council and peacekeeping powers, so that such wars would never happen again.

**UNICEF** — it provides for children's education, health, nutrition and protection, and often supplies desks, books and water facilities to schools. **UNESCO** — it promotes education, science and culture and supports schools with learning materials and teacher training. **Similarities:** both promote peace, human rights and development; both give technical assistance and scholarships; both hold regular meetings of member states; Uganda is a member of both. **Differences:** the UN has 193 members from the whole world while the Commonwealth has 56, mostly former British territories; the UN has peacekeeping forces while the Commonwealth has none; the UN is headquartered in New York and the Commonwealth in London; UN Security Council decisions can be binding, while Commonwealth decisions depend on goodwill.

The **veto** is the power held by each of the five permanent members of the Security Council — the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China — to block any decision, even when all the other members support it.
